What it is: A saturated carbon: four single bonds.
A carbon of a C=C double bond ("d" for double), as in an alkene.
A carbon of a C≡C triple bond ("t" for triple), as in an alkyne.
An aromatic carbon in a benzene ring ("B" for benzene).
A carbonyl carbon taken together with its oxygen, C=O.
A divalent oxygen: the oxygen of an ether, an alcohol or an ester.
An amine nitrogen: three single bonds.
The carbon of a nitrile, C≡N, taken together with its nitrogen.
The nitrogen of a nitro group, taken with its two oxygens.
A doubly-bonded imino nitrogen, as in an imine or an oxime. Contributes its nitrogen only; the carbon of the C=N is counted by its own `CdN` group.
The carbon of a C=N double bond — a `Cd` whose partner is nitrogen. Contributes its carbon only. See the note below.
An isocyanide, R–N≡C. The one value here is `NC-(C)`, and `C-(H)3(N)` + `NC-(C)` = −42 + 210 = 168 kJ/mol against a measured 163.5 ± 7.2 for methyl isocyanide.
The four ketene rows. How many heavy atoms they stand for is an open question, recorded in `notation/README.md`.
